entities.summary:
Abrocomes, a scion of the Achaemenid dynasty, was a son of Darius I, the Great King of Persia, and his wife Phratagune. Born into the heart of the world's most expansive empire around the late 6th century BCE, he was a half-brother to Xerxes I, who would later lead the colossal Persian invasion of Greece. Abrocomes' significance is primarily anchored in his participation in the Greco-Persian Wars, specifically his heroic—or tragic, depending on perspective—death at the pivotal Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BCE (though some accounts place his death at 479 BCE), a conflict that etched his name into the annals of ancient military history.

At Thermopylae, Abrocomes served as a commander within the vast Persian army assembled by Xerxes I, a force numbering in the hundreds of thousands. His presence on the battlefield underscored the personal commitment of the Achaemenid royal family to the conquest of Greece. According to Herodotus, Abrocomes, along with his full brother Hyperanthes, fell during the fierce fighting over the body of the Spartan king Leonidas I, a testament to the brutal intensity of the engagement. This act of attempting to retrieve or secure the body of a fallen enemy king highlights the ferocity and symbolic stakes of the battle, where even royal princes were not immune from the thick of the combat.

Abrocomes' death, alongside his brother, contributed to the narrative of Persian sacrifice and royal involvement in the Greco-Persian Wars. While his individual impact on the broader course of the war was limited by his early demise, his presence and death at Thermopylae served to emphasize the scale of the Persian commitment and the high cost of their imperial ambitions. His story, though brief, became a minor but vivid detail in the Greek historical accounts, underscoring the formidable opposition faced by the Hellenic city-states and the personal risks taken by the Persian royal house.
